subject: Health and Physical Education

sources.title: NZC Health and Physical Education Years 0–10, September 2026
sources.status: published-final; Gazette pending; proposed Years 9–10 from 2027, Years 0–8 from 2029; transition applies

topics.name: Everyday body care
topics.description: Everyday care can include washing hands, drinking water, resting and choosing clothing suited to the conditions. People may need different support.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: everyday body care.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Washing hands can help reduce the spread of germs to food and other people.
misconceptions: Germs cannot move from hands to things people touch.
topics.question: Why wash hands before preparing food?
topics.answer: Washing hands can help reduce the spread of germs to food and other people.
topics.explanation: Everyday care can include washing hands, drinking water, resting and choosing clothing suited to the conditions. People may need different support.
hints: Think about what hands touch.
How could germs move from hands to food?
topics.activity: Practise handwashing with soap and water and describe when it is useful.

topics.name: Asking for help and expressing boundaries
topics.description: People can communicate when they feel unsafe or uncomfortable and seek help from a trusted adult or appropriate support person.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: asking for help and expressing boundaries.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Move to a safer place if possible and tell a trusted adult or support person.
misconceptions: A person must keep an unsafe situation secret.
topics.question: What could a child do if a situation feels unsafe?
topics.answer: Move to a safer place if possible and tell a trusted adult or support person.
topics.explanation: People can communicate when they feel unsafe or uncomfortable and seek help from a trusted adult or appropriate support person.
hints: Who can help?
How could the child communicate that they are uncomfortable?
topics.activity: With a fictional scenario, identify two trusted support people and practise a simple request for help without sharing private details.

topics.name: Balance and body awareness
topics.description: Movement can involve holding positions, shifting weight and keeping balance while noticing the space and people around you.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11–12, Phase 1 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: balance and body awareness.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They can adjust their body position and base of support in a comfortable, safe way.
misconceptions: Balance cannot be changed by adjusting body position.
topics.question: What could help someone balance while standing still?
topics.answer: They can adjust their body position and base of support in a comfortable, safe way.
topics.explanation: Movement can involve holding positions, shifting weight and keeping balance while noticing the space and people around you.
hints: Notice where the feet contact the ground.
How could changing position affect stability?
topics.activity: In a clear space, try two comfortable standing positions with support available and describe how each feels.

topics.name: Moving safely with others
topics.description: Safe movement involves awareness of available space, other people, equipment and personal abilities.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11–12, Phase 1 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: moving safely with others.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It helps identify people or obstacles so the group can use the space more safely.
misconceptions: The same movement is safe in every space without checking it.
topics.question: Why look around before starting a running game?
topics.answer: It helps identify people or obstacles so the group can use the space more safely.
topics.explanation: Safe movement involves awareness of available space, other people, equipment and personal abilities.
hints: What else might be in the space?
How could a collision be avoided?
topics.activity: Set out a clear imaginary play area and identify a safe route and a way to stop when needed.

topics.name: Recognising feelings and support
topics.description: Feelings can change in response to experiences. People can describe feelings in different ways and seek support when they need it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14–16, Phase 2 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: recognising feelings and support.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They might talk with a trusted person and choose a calming strategy that works for them.
misconceptions: Everyone feels the same way about the same situation.
topics.question: What could someone do if they feel worried about a fictional situation?
topics.answer: They might talk with a trusted person and choose a calming strategy that works for them.
topics.explanation: Feelings can change in response to experiences. People can describe feelings in different ways and seek support when they need it.
hints: Who could listen and help?
What safe action could help them pause?
topics.activity: Use fictional scenarios to name a possible feeling and identify a supportive response without asking anyone to disclose personal experiences.

topics.name: Hygiene and shared wellbeing
topics.description: Hygiene practices can help reduce the spread of germs and support both individual and community wellbeing.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14–16, Phase 2 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: hygiene and shared wellbeing.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: These actions can reduce the spread of germs from one person to others.
misconceptions: Hygiene affects only the person performing it.
topics.question: How can covering a cough and washing hands help other people?
topics.answer: These actions can reduce the spread of germs from one person to others.
topics.explanation: Hygiene practices can help reduce the spread of germs and support both individual and community wellbeing.
hints: Consider what may be released during a cough.
What can clean hands help prevent?
topics.activity: Make a simple illustrated reminder of two hygiene actions and when to use them.

topics.name: Practising movement with feedback
topics.description: Movement skills develop with practice, observation and useful feedback. Activities can be adapted to different abilities and access needs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17–18, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: practising movement with feedback.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A specific observation such as “Try facing the target and releasing towards it” may help.
misconceptions: Useful feedback only says whether someone is good at sport.
topics.question: What feedback could help someone improve a beanbag throw?
topics.answer: A specific observation such as “Try facing the target and releasing towards it” may help.
topics.explanation: Movement skills develop with practice, observation and useful feedback. Activities can be adapted to different abilities and access needs.
hints: Describe one part of the movement.
Suggest one small change to try.
topics.activity: Practise a gentle beanbag throw toward a nearby target and adjust the distance or action to suit the learner.

topics.name: Cooperation in games
topics.description: Players can use rules, communication and shared decisions to make a game inclusive and enjoyable.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17–18, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cooperation in games.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could adjust equipment, rules, pace or roles with participants' input.
misconceptions: A fair game requires identical participation without considering access needs.
topics.question: How could a group adapt a game so more people can participate?
topics.answer: They could adjust equipment, rules, pace or roles with participants' input.
topics.explanation: Players can use rules, communication and shared decisions to make a game inclusive and enjoyable.
hints: What part of the game makes participation difficult?
Can the group change a rule or piece of equipment?
topics.activity: Design a fictional game and agree on one adaptation that gives more players a meaningful role.

topics.name: Consent and personal boundaries
topics.description: Respectful relationships involve recognising boundaries, asking permission and accepting a person's response. Permission can be withdrawn.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20–21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: consent and personal boundaries.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Stop and respect their decision.
misconceptions: Someone must continue to agree because they agreed earlier.
topics.question: A friend says they no longer want a hug. What is a respectful response?
topics.answer: Stop and respect their decision.
topics.explanation: Respectful relationships involve recognising boundaries, asking permission and accepting a person's response. Permission can be withdrawn.
hints: What did the person communicate?
Does previous agreement require them to continue?
topics.activity: Practise asking and responding respectfully using a fictional non-personal example, such as borrowing an object.

topics.name: Checking health information
topics.description: Health information can vary in reliability. A learner can check the source, evidence and date and seek appropriate adult or professional support.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20–21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: checking health information.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Check who made the claim, whether reliable evidence supports it and whether current authoritative guidance agrees.
misconceptions: A health claim is reliable merely because it has been shared many times.
topics.question: A social-media post makes a health claim without a source. What should a reader check?
topics.answer: Check who made the claim, whether reliable evidence supports it and whether current authoritative guidance agrees.
topics.explanation: Health information can vary in reliability. A learner can check the source, evidence and date and seek appropriate adult or professional support.
hints: Who produced the claim?
Where could the evidence be checked?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional health claims and identify the information needed to check each; do not diagnose anyone.

topics.name: Activity intensity and duration
topics.description: How hard and how long a person moves can affect effort and recovery. People can respond differently and adapt activity to their needs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22–23, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: activity intensity and duration.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A longer activity can require sustained effort over time; individual responses vary.
misconceptions: All people respond identically to the same physical activity.
topics.question: How might a longer activity differ from a short burst of movement?
topics.answer: A longer activity can require sustained effort over time; individual responses vary.
topics.explanation: How hard and how long a person moves can affect effort and recovery. People can respond differently and adapt activity to their needs.
hints: Compare how long each activity lasts.
Does each activity make the same demand over time?
topics.activity: Plan two fictional activities of different duration and describe how a participant might adjust pace and rest.

topics.name: Making decisions in games
topics.description: Players can observe the position of teammates, opponents and space and choose actions that support a shared goal.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22–23, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: making decisions in games.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The teammate may have more time or room to continue the play.
misconceptions: A player should always make the same move regardless of the situation.
topics.question: Why might a player pass to a teammate in an open space?
topics.answer: The teammate may have more time or room to continue the play.
topics.explanation: Players can observe the position of teammates, opponents and space and choose actions that support a shared goal.
hints: Where is the open space?
Who is able to receive the pass?
topics.activity: Sketch a simple game situation and discuss two possible passes and their trade-offs.

topics.name: Models of wellbeing
topics.description: Different models can help people consider connected aspects of wellbeing. Each model has its own context and should be studied with reliable, attributed guidance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25–27, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: models of wellbeing.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Relationships can influence how people feel and function alongside physical and other aspects of wellbeing.
misconceptions: Wellbeing is determined by physical health alone.
topics.question: Why might a wellbeing model consider relationships as well as physical health?
topics.answer: Relationships can influence how people feel and function alongside physical and other aspects of wellbeing.
topics.explanation: Different models can help people consider connected aspects of wellbeing. Each model has its own context and should be studied with reliable, attributed guidance.
hints: Think about social support.
Could wellbeing involve more than the body alone?
topics.activity: Compare two appropriately attributed wellbeing models and identify one aspect each includes without treating either as universal.

topics.name: Influences on health decisions
topics.description: Health-related decisions can be influenced by family, culture, access, cost, media and personal circumstances. These factors vary between people.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25–27, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: influences on health decisions.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Their preferences, culture, access, cost and circumstances may differ.
misconceptions: People make health choices independently of their circumstances.
topics.question: Why might two people make different food choices even when given the same information?
topics.answer: Their preferences, culture, access, cost and circumstances may differ.
topics.explanation: Health-related decisions can be influenced by family, culture, access, cost, media and personal circumstances. These factors vary between people.
hints: What resources are available to each person?
What other influences might matter?
topics.activity: Analyse a fictional food advertisement for its intended audience and one influence it might have, without judging personal eating.

topics.name: Stability and base of support
topics.description: Balance and stability depend partly on body position and the base of support. The effect of a change depends on the person and activity.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28–29, Phase 4 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: stability and base of support.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can increase the base of support, depending on posture and the movement involved.
misconceptions: Balance never depends on the body's position or support.
topics.question: Why might a wider stance help a person feel more stable?
topics.answer: It can increase the base of support, depending on posture and the movement involved.
topics.explanation: Balance and stability depend partly on body position and the base of support. The effect of a change depends on the person and activity.
hints: Where does the body contact the ground?
Compare the area between the points of support.
topics.activity: In a safe seated or standing position suited to the learner, compare two bases of support and describe any difference.

topics.name: Planning for activity risks
topics.description: Planning an outdoor or physical activity includes identifying hazards, considering participants and choosing suitable precautions and supervision.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28–29, Phase 4 > Physical Education; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: planning for activity risks.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could check weather, route, group needs, equipment and a plan for getting help.
misconceptions: A familiar activity never needs any safety planning.
topics.question: Before an outdoor walk, what could a group check?
topics.answer: They could check weather, route, group needs, equipment and a plan for getting help.
topics.explanation: Planning an outdoor or physical activity includes identifying hazards, considering participants and choosing suitable precautions and supervision.
hints: What conditions could change outdoors?
How would the group communicate if plans change?
topics.activity: Review a fictional walk plan, identify two possible hazards and suggest appropriate precautions with an adult.

topics.name: Rest and growing bodies
topics.description: Rest and sleep help a growing body recover and support how people feel and function. Sleep needs and routines differ between people.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Health, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate rest and growing bodies using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They could rest and follow a suitable sleep routine with support from a trusted adult.
misconceptions: Rest is useful only after someone becomes ill.
topics.question: A fictional child is tired after a busy day. What is one supportive choice?
topics.answer: They could rest and follow a suitable sleep routine with support from a trusted adult.
topics.explanation: Rest gives the body time to recover and can support attention and wellbeing.
hints: Think about what the body may need after a busy day.
What could help it recover before tomorrow?
topics.activity: Make a picture schedule for a fictional character that includes a quiet wind-down and a time for rest.

topics.name: Household substances and supervision
topics.description: Some medicines and cleaning products can cause harm if used incorrectly. Children should leave them to a responsible adult and follow household safety instructions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Health, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate household substances and supervision using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Leave it closed and ask a trusted adult for help.
misconceptions: Every household product is safe for a child to use alone.
topics.question: A child finds an unknown cleaning bottle. What should they do?
topics.answer: Leave it closed and ask a trusted adult for help.
topics.explanation: A responsible adult can identify the substance and use the label and safety instructions.
hints: Does the child know what is in the bottle?
Who can handle household products safely?
topics.activity: Use drawings of everyday products to practise identifying which items should be left for an adult; keep real substances closed and out of reach.

topics.name: Noticing food advertising
topics.description: Advertising tries to influence choices using images, words and placement. Food decisions are also shaped by access, preference and whānau practices.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Health, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate noticing food advertising using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Ask who made the advertisement, what it is trying to sell and what information supports the claim.
misconceptions: An attractive food advertisement proves every claim it makes.
topics.question: A colourful advertisement calls a snack “the best”. What is useful to ask?
topics.answer: Ask who made the advertisement, what it is trying to sell and what information supports the claim.
topics.explanation: Persuasive design shows the advertiser's purpose; it does not establish that a claim is accurate.
hints: Who wants someone to buy the snack?
Which words are trying to persuade the reader?
topics.activity: Invent a food advertisement on paper and circle one persuasive feature, then write one question a reader could ask.

topics.name: Kind communication and friendships
topics.description: Kind communication can include listening, taking turns and respecting another person's response. People may communicate in spoken, signed or other ways.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Health, Year 1
objectives: Explain or demonstrate kind communication and friendships using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Pause, give them time and respond to what they communicate.
misconceptions: A person is listening only if they speak at the same time.
topics.question: A classmate wants a turn to speak or sign. What could another person do?
topics.answer: Pause, give them time and respond to what they communicate.
topics.explanation: Allowing a person time and responding respectfully helps them participate.
hints: Who has not yet had a turn?
How could the listener show they are attending?
topics.activity: Use fictional role cards to practise taking turns communicating and responding without asking children to share personal experiences.

topics.name: Responding to upsetting online content
topics.description: A child who encounters upsetting or confusing online content can stop viewing it and seek help from a trusted adult. They do not need to investigate or share it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Phase 1 > Health, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to upsetting online content using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Stop viewing it and tell a trusted adult.
misconceptions: A child must solve an upsetting online situation alone.
topics.question: A fictional child sees something frightening online. What is one safe next step?
topics.answer: Stop viewing it and tell a trusted adult.
topics.explanation: A supportive adult can help assess the situation without the child having to handle the material alone.
hints: Should the child keep exploring the upsetting content?
Who could help them?
topics.activity: Discuss a made-up situation with no real images and identify a trusted adult and a simple way to ask for help.

topics.name: Responding to bullying safely
topics.description: Bullying can harm belonging and wellbeing. Safe responses may include seeking adult support and following agreed school procedures.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Phase 1 > Health, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to bullying safely using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Seek help from a trusted adult and support the classmate if it is safe to do so.
misconceptions: The person being bullied has to stop the bullying without help.
topics.question: A fictional classmate is repeatedly excluded and threatened. What could another learner do?
topics.answer: Seek help from a trusted adult and support the classmate if it is safe to do so.
topics.explanation: A community response can interrupt harmful behaviour without requiring a child to confront danger alone.
hints: Is the behaviour happening repeatedly?
Who can help make the situation safer?
topics.activity: Use a fictional scenario to list one safe supportive action and one adult or school support route.

topics.name: Preparing for movement
topics.description: Starting gently can help prepare muscles and joints before more demanding movement. Everyone can adapt activities to their abilities and needs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate preparing for movement using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Gentle movement helps the body prepare for the activity.
misconceptions: A warm-up must be fast and uncomfortable to be useful.
topics.question: Why might a group begin an activity with gentle movements?
topics.answer: Gentle movement helps the body prepare for the activity.
topics.explanation: Gentle movement increases readiness gradually and can be adapted to the activity and person.
hints: Compare starting slowly with starting at full effort.
What might help muscles and joints get ready?
topics.activity: In a clear space, invite learners to try comfortable shoulder and leg movements or a seated equivalent before a gentle game.

topics.name: Throwing towards a target
topics.description: Aiming involves directing an object towards a chosen target while considering safety and other people in the space.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate throwing towards a target using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Adjust the direction of the throw and try again from a comfortable distance.
misconceptions: One missed attempt means a movement skill cannot improve.
topics.question: A beanbag misses a target to the left. What could the learner try next?
topics.answer: Adjust the direction of the throw and try again from a comfortable distance.
topics.explanation: Changing direction responds to where the object landed; safe practice gives the learner another observation.
hints: Which side of the target did it miss?
Which way could the next throw be adjusted?
topics.activity: Roll or gently toss a soft object towards a nearby target, adjusting distance and method for the learner.

topics.name: Recognising water hazards and signs
topics.description: Water environments differ, and signs, flags and adult guidance can help people identify local hazards. Water practice needs suitable supervision.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising water hazards and signs using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Follow the warning and seek local advice or choose a safer activity.
misconceptions: Water is safe wherever it looks calm.
topics.question: A beach has a warning sign about a hazard. What should a family do?
topics.answer: Follow the warning and seek local advice or choose a safer activity.
topics.explanation: Warning signs communicate a hazard, and local advice can account for conditions that are not obvious.
hints: What does a warning sign ask people to notice?
Who can explain the local conditions?
topics.activity: On paper, match fictional pool or beach signs with their messages and discuss seeking adult guidance; no water entry is needed.

topics.name: Using landmarks on a familiar route
topics.description: Signs, simple maps and landmarks can help people describe where they are and follow an agreed route within safe boundaries.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12, Phase 1 > Physical Education, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate using landmarks on a familiar route using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The large tree, if it is a clear and reliable landmark on the map and in the place.
misconceptions: A map cannot use landmarks to help someone locate themselves.
topics.question: A map shows a playground next to a large tree. Which feature could help a walker confirm their location?
topics.answer: The large tree, if it is a clear and reliable landmark on the map and in the place.
topics.explanation: A feature visible both on the map and on the route can help the group recognise its position.
hints: Look for a feature shown on both the map and the ground.
Which feature is next to the playground?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional park route with a start, finish and two landmarks; identify the agreed safe boundary.

topics.name: Finding reliable nutrition information
topics.description: Food choices are influenced by taste, access, culture, cost and advertising. Reliable information can support choices without judging a person's circumstances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 > Health, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate finding reliable nutrition information using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Check the ingredient list and nutrition information alongside relevant trusted guidance and individual needs.
misconceptions: A single advertising word is enough to judge a food's nutritional information.
topics.question: A package advertises a food as “amazing”. What information could be more useful to check?
topics.answer: Check the ingredient list and nutrition information alongside relevant trusted guidance and individual needs.
topics.explanation: A label supplies specific information that can be considered with trustworthy guidance rather than relying on promotional language.
hints: What factual information is printed on the package?
Does a promotional word explain the ingredients?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional labels for their stated ingredients and discuss how access and preferences can affect a choice.

topics.name: Puberty and variation
topics.description: Puberty involves physical and emotional changes as bodies mature. It can begin at different ages, and people experience changes at different rates.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 > Health, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate puberty and variation using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: No. The timing and experience of puberty vary; a trusted health professional can answer individual concerns.
misconceptions: Everyone begins puberty at the same age and follows an identical timeline.
topics.question: Two fictional young people begin growing at different times. Does that mean one is automatically unhealthy?
topics.answer: No. The timing and experience of puberty vary; a trusted health professional can answer individual concerns.
topics.explanation: Development varies across people, so a single timeline is not a reliable benchmark for everyone.
hints: Do all bodies grow at the same rate?
Who can give advice about an individual health concern?
topics.activity: Use a fictional timeline with a range of starting points to discuss variation; do not ask learners to disclose their own changes.

topics.name: Understanding menstruation
topics.description: Menstruation is part of the menstrual cycle for some people. Experiences vary, and reliable information and supportive adults can help with questions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 > Health, Year 6
objectives: Explain or demonstrate understanding menstruation using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Offer practical support or help them contact a trusted adult, while respecting privacy.
misconceptions: Everyone has the same menstrual experience or needs to discuss it publicly.
topics.question: What is one way to support a fictional student who needs menstrual supplies?
topics.answer: Offer practical support or help them contact a trusted adult, while respecting privacy.
topics.explanation: Practical help respects the student’s needs without assuming that they want to share private information.
hints: What practical item might the student need?
How can help be offered without embarrassing them?
topics.activity: Use a fictional school scenario to identify where someone could find supplies and trustworthy information; no personal disclosure is needed.

topics.name: Stereotypes and inclusion
topics.description: A stereotype assigns a generalised trait to a group and can lead to unfair assumptions about individuals.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 > Health, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate stereotypes and inclusion using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It assumes an interest based on gender instead of recognising that individuals differ.
misconceptions: A group stereotype accurately describes every individual in that group.
topics.question: A fictional classmate says that only boys can enjoy science. What makes this a stereotype?
topics.answer: It assumes an interest based on gender instead of recognising that individuals differ.
topics.explanation: The claim assigns a preference to every member of a gender group without considering individuals.
hints: Is the claim about one person's interest or a whole group?
Can people of different genders enjoy the same subject?
topics.activity: Rewrite two fictional stereotypes as statements that leave room for individual differences.

topics.name: Consent, pressure and silence
topics.description: Consent is a voluntary and informed agreement. Silence or pressure does not establish that someone agrees, and a person can change their mind.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 > Health, Year 6
objectives: Explain or demonstrate consent, pressure and silence using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: No. Silence does not show voluntary, informed agreement.
misconceptions: Silence or pressure counts as clear permission.
topics.question: A person stays silent while another keeps asking to borrow their phone. Has the person clearly agreed?
topics.answer: No. Silence does not show voluntary, informed agreement.
topics.explanation: A voluntary agreement must be expressed; repeated pressure or lack of response does not establish it.
hints: What words or actions would show a clear response?
Does repeated pressure make silence into agreement?
topics.activity: Practise fictional responses to a request to borrow an object, including asking, refusing and accepting the answer.

topics.name: Medicine and trusted adult guidance
topics.description: Medicines can help when used as directed, but the wrong medicine or dose can cause harm. Children should seek a responsible adult's guidance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate medicine and trusted adult guidance using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: No. Leave it alone and ask a trusted adult or health professional for guidance.
misconceptions: A medicine is safe for everyone whenever it helped someone else.
topics.question: A fictional child finds a medicine that belongs to someone else. Should they take it?
topics.answer: No. Leave it alone and ask a trusted adult or health professional for guidance.
topics.explanation: A medicine prescribed for one person may be inappropriate or unsafe for another.
hints: Whose medicine is it?
Can a child know the correct use without guidance?
topics.activity: Create a fictional label with a reminder to ask an adult; do not handle or taste real medicines.

topics.name: Receiving and passing with control
topics.description: Movement skills can be practised by observing a target, adjusting force and coordinating with a partner. Activities should be adapted to the participants.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate receiving and passing with control using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Use less force, increase the distance or choose a slower way to send the object.
misconceptions: More force always makes a pass easier to receive.
topics.question: A soft pass reaches a partner too quickly to catch. What could be adjusted?
topics.answer: Use less force, increase the distance or choose a slower way to send the object.
topics.explanation: A gentler or slower pass gives the receiver more time to track and control the object.
hints: How fast did the object arrive?
What would give the partner more time?
topics.activity: With a soft ball or rolled-up socks, practise passing at a comfortable distance and let either person request an adaptation.

topics.name: Staying afloat with supervision
topics.description: Floating is a water-survival skill, but people float differently and need instruction and appropriate supervision. Water conditions and personal abilities matter.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate staying afloat with supervision using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A supervised setting can account for the learner's ability and the conditions while providing appropriate assistance.
misconceptions: Everyone floats the same way and can safely practise alone.
topics.question: Why should a learner practise water skills with a qualified instructor and suitable supervision?
topics.answer: A supervised setting can account for the learner's ability and the conditions while providing appropriate assistance.
topics.explanation: A qualified supervisor can account for conditions, individual needs and access to assistance.
hints: Can water conditions and abilities vary?
Who can teach and supervise the skill safely?
topics.activity: Discuss an illustrated pool-safety plan, identifying supervision and an exit point; practise in water only in an appropriately supervised lesson.

topics.name: Preparing for an outdoor activity
topics.description: Outdoor preparation can include checking the planned route, weather, clothing, water and group needs, then adjusting the plan when conditions change.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate preparing for an outdoor activity using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Review the route and conditions, choose suitable clothing and decide whether the plan remains appropriate.
misconceptions: The same clothing and route are suitable in all weather.
topics.question: Rain is forecast for a fictional walk. What could the group check before leaving?
topics.answer: Review the route and conditions, choose suitable clothing and decide whether the plan remains appropriate.
topics.explanation: Weather can change the route and equipment needed, so the plan should reflect the actual conditions.
hints: What could change on the route in rain?
What clothing or alternative plan may be needed?
topics.activity: Use a fictional park walk to make a checklist for weather, clothing, drinking water and a trusted adult's plan.

topics.name: Consent before sharing digital content
topics.description: A person's agreement to be photographed or recorded does not automatically mean they agree to sharing the content. They can refuse or change their mind.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate consent before sharing digital content using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Respect the request and do not post the photo.
misconceptions: Permission to take a photo automatically permits sharing it everywhere.
topics.question: A friend agrees to a photo but asks that it not be posted. What should the photographer do?
topics.answer: Respect the request and do not post the photo.
topics.explanation: Permission applies to the particular action agreed to; taking an image and posting it are separate decisions.
hints: What did the friend agree to?
Did they agree to posting it?
topics.activity: Use a fictional photo scenario to practise asking separately about taking, keeping and sharing an image; do not collect real photos.

topics.name: Recognising less visible bullying
topics.description: Bullying can include repeated social exclusion, rumours or online behaviour as well as obvious physical actions. Support should be sought when a situation is unsafe.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising less visible bullying using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Yes. Repeated exclusion and rumours can harm wellbeing; a trusted adult or school process can help.
misconceptions: Bullying only counts when it is physical or visible to everyone.
topics.question: A fictional student is repeatedly excluded from a group chat and targeted by rumours. Could this be harmful?
topics.answer: Yes. Repeated exclusion and rumours can harm wellbeing; a trusted adult or school process can help.
topics.explanation: Repeated social exclusion and rumours can harm a person even when there is no physical contact.
hints: Does bullying have to be physical?
Is the behaviour repeated and targeted?
topics.activity: Consider a fictional scenario and identify one safe way to support the student and one appropriate help route.

topics.name: Communication during conflict
topics.description: A respectful response to conflict can include describing the issue, listening to the other person and seeking help when needed.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate communication during conflict using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Each can explain their view, listen to the other and agree on a workable next step or seek support.
misconceptions: Listening to another view means a person must give up all their own boundaries.
topics.question: Two fictional friends disagree about a shared plan. What could help them resolve the disagreement?
topics.answer: Each can explain their view, listen to the other and agree on a workable next step or seek support.
topics.explanation: Listening to different views can reveal a workable next step while each person retains their boundaries.
hints: Has each person had a chance to explain?
What shared step could they consider?
topics.activity: Use a fictional disagreement to practise one listening phrase and one proposal for a fair next step.

topics.name: Influences on substance decisions
topics.description: Decisions about alcohol, nicotine and other drugs can be affected by social pressure, advertising, information and personal circumstances. Learners can seek trusted, age-appropriate guidance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate influences on substance decisions using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Question the unsupported claim and the advertiser's purpose; reliable health information can provide context.
misconceptions: An advertisement accurately describes what every person does.
topics.question: A fictional advertisement suggests everyone uses a nicotine product. What should a viewer question?
topics.answer: Question the unsupported claim and the advertiser's purpose; reliable health information can provide context.
topics.explanation: Advertising has a persuasive purpose and its general claim is not independent evidence about people’s choices.
hints: Who benefits if viewers believe the advertisement?
Does the advertisement provide evidence about everyone?
topics.activity: Annotate a made-up advertisement to identify one persuasive tactic and one question for an independent source.

topics.name: Responding to discriminatory exclusion
topics.description: Stereotypes and exclusion can damage belonging. Inclusive communities involve shared responsibility, respectful participation and support.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to discriminatory exclusion using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Challenge the assumption safely, include the student and seek adult support when appropriate.
misconceptions: An assumption about a group describes every individual in that group.
topics.question: A fictional student is excluded because of an assumption about their culture. What could peers do?
topics.answer: Challenge the assumption safely, include the student and seek adult support when appropriate.
topics.explanation: Inclusion responds to an unfair assumption and support can help address exclusion safely.
hints: What assumption is being made about the student?
Who can help create an inclusive response?
topics.activity: Use fictional role cards to plan one inclusive action and one support step without asking learners to describe personal discrimination.

topics.name: Speed, timing and movement control
topics.description: The speed and timing of a movement can affect accuracy and control. Learners can adapt their actions after observing a result.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate speed, timing and movement control using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Slow the movement or adjust timing, then compare the result.
misconceptions: Moving as fast as possible always produces the most accurate result.
topics.question: A learner misses a target when moving very quickly. What could they try?
topics.answer: Slow the movement or adjust timing, then compare the result.
topics.explanation: Changing one controllable feature enables the learner to compare how it affects accuracy.
hints: How did speed affect control?
What happens if the learner changes one part of the movement?
topics.activity: Roll a soft object towards a target at two comfortable speeds and compare control, adapting the task as needed.

topics.name: Coordinating roles in a game
topics.description: Players can use communication and awareness to coordinate roles and respond to changing game situations.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22–23, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate coordinating roles in a game using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Shared roles can help participants coordinate actions and understand how each person can contribute.
misconceptions: A team can coordinate only if everyone performs exactly the same role.
topics.question: Why might teammates agree on roles before a modified game?
topics.answer: Shared roles can help participants coordinate actions and understand how each person can contribute.
topics.explanation: Clear, flexible roles help players understand how to coordinate without requiring identical contributions.
hints: Who is doing each task?
How could a shared plan help people work together?
topics.activity: Design a small fictional game and assign flexible roles that allow every player to participate.

topics.name: Water conditions and safe decisions
topics.description: Water safety decisions depend on conditions such as depth, currents, temperature, weather and supervision. Skills learned in one setting do not automatically make another setting safe.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate water conditions and safe decisions using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A beach can have changing waves, currents and conditions that differ from a supervised pool.
misconceptions: Being comfortable in a pool makes every open-water situation safe.
topics.question: Why might a learner who swims in a pool need extra guidance at a beach?
topics.answer: A beach can have changing waves, currents and conditions that differ from a supervised pool.
topics.explanation: Open water can involve hazards and changing conditions that are absent in a supervised pool.
hints: Is the water environment the same?
Which beach conditions could change?
topics.activity: Compare a fictional pool and beach using illustrated signs, hazards and appropriate supervision; do not enter the water for this task.
materials: illustrations of pool and beach hazards

topics.name: Navigation and changing conditions
topics.description: Outdoor participants can use route information, landmarks and group communication while adjusting plans for weather and terrain.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate navigation and changing conditions using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Stop, follow the closure and use the agreed safer alternative or seek appropriate guidance.
misconceptions: A planned route should always be followed even when conditions make it unsafe.
topics.question: A planned path is closed because of flooding. What should a group do?
topics.answer: Stop, follow the closure and use the agreed safer alternative or seek appropriate guidance.
topics.explanation: A closure signals that the original route needs review, and the alternative plan supports a safer decision.
hints: What does the closure tell the group?
Should the original plan continue unchanged?
topics.activity: Review a fictional route map and create a decision point for changed weather, closure or a participant needing support.

topics.name: Identity, belonging and wellbeing
topics.description: People's identities can include many characteristics, relationships and interests. Respect and belonging can support wellbeing, while stigma or exclusion can harm it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate identity, belonging and wellbeing using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Being accepted and able to participate can support connection and wellbeing.
misconceptions: Everyone with the same identity has the same experiences or interests.
topics.question: Why might an inclusive group improve a fictional student's sense of belonging?
topics.answer: Being accepted and able to participate can support connection and wellbeing.
topics.explanation: Acceptance and accessible participation can support social connection; different people experience belonging differently.
hints: Can a person have more than one interest or group?
How might being respected affect participation?
topics.activity: Review a fictional school group and propose two ways to make participation welcoming without requiring anyone to disclose identity details.

topics.name: Responding to pressure about substances
topics.description: Peer pressure and advertising can influence decisions about alcohol and other drugs. Assertive communication and trusted guidance can support safer choices.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to pressure about substances using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They can say no clearly, leave the situation if safe and seek support from someone they trust.
misconceptions: Someone must accept a substance to remain part of a group.
topics.question: A fictional teenager is pressured to drink alcohol. What is one assertive response?
topics.answer: They can say no clearly, leave the situation if safe and seek support from someone they trust.
topics.explanation: An assertive refusal and a safe exit uphold the person’s choice and provide a route to support.
hints: Does the person have to accept the offer?
What could they say or do to maintain their boundary?
topics.activity: Practise fictional refusal phrases and a plan to contact support; do not ask anyone to disclose personal substance use.

topics.name: Protective factors during change
topics.description: Supportive relationships, helpful routines and access to appropriate services can help people cope with change. What helps varies by person and situation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate protective factors during change using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A trusted person, a welcoming group or access to appropriate school support may help.
misconceptions: A person must manage every major change alone.
topics.question: A fictional person is unsettled by a change of school. What could be a protective support?
topics.answer: A trusted person, a welcoming group or access to appropriate school support may help.
topics.explanation: Supportive relationships and access to help can reduce isolation during a difficult change.
hints: Who could listen and offer support?
What could help the person feel connected?
topics.activity: Make a support map for a fictional character facing a change, including peers, trusted adults and relevant services.

topics.name: Responding to cyberbullying
topics.description: Harmful online behaviour can affect wellbeing. A person can seek support, use platform controls and preserve information for appropriate reporting when safe.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to cyberbullying using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Seek trusted support, use available block or report tools and avoid responding to the harm if that feels unsafe.
misconceptions: Cyberbullying cannot cause harm because it occurs online.
topics.question: A fictional learner receives repeated harmful messages. What is a safer next step?
topics.answer: Seek trusted support, use available block or report tools and avoid responding to the harm if that feels unsafe.
topics.explanation: A trusted person can help, while platform controls can limit contact and report harmful behaviour.
hints: Who can help the learner?
Which platform tools can limit further contact?
topics.activity: Using a fictional app interface, identify the block and report actions and a trusted support route; do not open real harmful messages.

topics.name: Privacy and online boundaries
topics.description: Privacy settings and careful sharing can reduce exposure, although no setting guarantees control over how others use information.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate privacy and online boundaries using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Sharing can affect the friend's privacy and the information may be copied or reach an unexpected audience.
misconceptions: A privacy setting guarantees that a post can never be copied or shared.
topics.question: Why think before posting a friend's personal information?
topics.answer: Sharing can affect the friend's privacy and the information may be copied or reach an unexpected audience.
topics.explanation: Once information is shared, other people may copy or forward it even if privacy settings are enabled.
hints: Whose information is it?
Can an online post be copied or forwarded?
topics.activity: Review a fictional profile and choose two details to keep private; discuss asking before sharing someone else's information.

topics.name: Boundaries and pressure in relationships
topics.description: Healthy relationships involve mutual respect, communication and boundaries. Pressure or manipulation can make it difficult to make a free choice.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate boundaries and pressure in relationships using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Stop pressuring them, respect their response and allow them to decide freely.
misconceptions: A person must agree to keep a relationship respectful.
topics.question: A fictional person feels pressured to agree to something they do not want. What should a respectful partner do?
topics.answer: Stop pressuring them, respect their response and allow them to decide freely.
topics.explanation: A freely made decision requires space to refuse without repeated pressure or punishment.
hints: Is the choice free if someone keeps pressuring them?
What does respecting the other person's answer involve?
topics.activity: Use a fictional non-explicit scenario to practise recognising pressure and identifying a trusted source of support.

topics.name: Forces and movement technique
topics.description: Forces acting on the body or equipment can affect movement, speed and direction. Technique can be adapted to the person and task.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 4 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate forces and movement technique using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The force acts in a different direction and can change the ball's motion.
misconceptions: A force cannot change the direction of movement.
topics.question: Why might changing the direction of a push change where a ball rolls?
topics.answer: The force acts in a different direction and can change the ball's motion.
topics.explanation: A push applies force in a direction, which can alter how the object moves.
hints: Which way is the push applied?
Compare that direction with the ball's path.
topics.activity: In a clear space, gently roll a soft ball in two directions and describe the force and resulting paths.

topics.name: Components of movement performance
topics.description: Agility, balance, coordination, speed, power and reaction time describe different aspects of movement performance. Their importance depends on the activity.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 4 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate components of movement performance using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Reaction time describes how quickly the participant responds to the signal.
misconceptions: One measure describes every aspect of movement performance.
topics.question: Which component helps a participant respond promptly to a start signal?
topics.answer: Reaction time describes how quickly the participant responds to the signal.
topics.explanation: Reaction time measures the delay between noticing a signal and initiating a response.
hints: What occurs between the signal and the response?
Which component relates to responding?
topics.activity: Discuss a fictional activity and choose two relevant movement components, allowing for different ways to participate.

topics.name: Shared responsibility in outdoor planning
topics.description: Outdoor planning includes participants' abilities, environmental conditions, communication and a response if the plan changes. Decisions belong to the supervised group.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate shared responsibility in outdoor planning using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Pause safely, check the person's needs and the conditions, and use the agreed support or alternative plan.
misconceptions: A group should continue its original plan regardless of participants' needs.
topics.question: On a fictional group walk one participant becomes tired and conditions worsen. What should the group consider?
topics.answer: Pause safely, check the person's needs and the conditions, and use the agreed support or alternative plan.
topics.explanation: Responding to a participant’s needs and changing conditions supports the agreed safety plan.
hints: What has changed for the participant?
How does the group plan account for changed conditions?
topics.activity: Create a fictional group plan with roles, a weather check and a decision point for changing or stopping the activity.

topics.name: Food variety and nourishment
topics.description: Foods provide different nutrients that help growing bodies function. People and whānau make food choices in different circumstances, including differing access, tastes and traditions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 > Health, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate food variety and nourishment using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Different foods can contribute different nutrients needed by the body.
misconceptions: A healthy meal must be identical for every person or family.
topics.question: A fictional lunch includes a range of foods. Why can variety be useful?
topics.answer: Different foods can contribute different nutrients needed by the body.
topics.explanation: No one food provides every nutrient in the same way, and the overall pattern of available foods matters.
hints: Do all foods contain the same nutrients?
What might a selection of foods provide together?
topics.activity: Sort fictional food pictures into different types and describe how several foods can contribute to a meal without labelling a person's food as good or bad.

topics.name: Protecting personal information
topics.description: Keeping personal information safer can include using appropriate privacy settings, logging out of shared devices and not sharing passwords. A trusted adult can help choose settings.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 > Health, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate protecting personal information using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Log out of the account and avoid leaving the password available to others.
misconceptions: A password is safe to share with anyone who asks for it online.
topics.question: A student finishes using a shared device. What should they do to protect their account?
topics.answer: Log out of the account and avoid leaving the password available to others.
topics.explanation: Logging out reduces the chance that the next person can access the account as that student.
hints: Is the device used by one person or many?
What should happen to the account session before the next user arrives?
topics.activity: Use a fictional account checklist to mark which information should stay private and where to log out; do not ask anyone to reveal real passwords.

topics.name: Managing feelings during change
topics.description: Changes at home, at school or in other parts of life can bring different feelings. People may seek support, use calming strategies or talk to a trusted person without having to disclose more than they choose.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 > Health, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate managing feelings during change using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They could talk to a trusted person or use an agreed calming strategy.
misconceptions: Everyone reacts to the same change in the same way.
topics.question: A fictional student feels overwhelmed after changing schools. What is one supportive action?
topics.answer: They could talk to a trusted person or use an agreed calming strategy.
topics.explanation: Support and coping strategies can help someone manage a difficult change while respecting their privacy.
hints: Who could offer a listening ear?
What safe action might help the student feel calmer?
topics.activity: Create a fictional character and choose two coping or support options for a change; let participants pass on sharing personal experiences.

topics.name: Recognising online engagement prompts
topics.description: Digital platforms may use notifications, likes and rewards to encourage people to keep using them. Recognising these prompts can help people decide how to use their time and attention.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 > Health, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising online engagement prompts using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They could recognise the prompts and choose a limit or adjust notification settings with appropriate support.
misconceptions: Every notification is necessary and must be opened immediately.
topics.question: An app repeatedly sends rewards and notifications to bring users back. What could a user consider?
topics.answer: They could recognise the prompts and choose a limit or adjust notification settings with appropriate support.
topics.explanation: Recognising a design feature helps a person make a deliberate choice about continued use.
hints: What happens when the person stops using the app?
Which controls might reduce interruptions?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional app screen, label two features designed to attract attention and propose one way a user could respond.

topics.name: Recognising online grooming warning signs
topics.description: Someone online may try to build trust with a young person in order to exploit them. Requests for secrecy, sexual images or an in-person meeting are warning signs; a trusted adult or specialist support service can help.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 > Health, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising online grooming warning signs using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Do not send the image, stop engaging and seek help from a trusted adult or specialist support service.
misconceptions: A person must handle threatening or exploitative messages alone to avoid getting in trouble.
topics.question: A fictional online contact asks a student to keep their messages secret and send an intimate image. What is a safer response?
topics.answer: Do not send the image, stop engaging and seek help from a trusted adult or specialist support service.
topics.explanation: An adult or specialist can help with the situation; the student does not need to handle pressure alone.
hints: Does the student have to comply with a request for secrecy or an image?
Who could help the student safely?
topics.activity: Use a fictional message with no explicit content to identify the request, a boundary and a route to trusted help; do not collect or display actual messages.

topics.name: Media messages and body image
topics.description: Images and comments in media can shape how people think about bodies. Images may be selected or altered, and bodies naturally differ; respectful discussion avoids judging appearance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 > Health, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate media messages and body image using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The image may be edited or selected and cannot represent the diversity of real bodies.
misconceptions: A single media image describes how everyone should look.
topics.question: A fictional post claims every person should look like a heavily edited photo. What is one reason to question it?
topics.answer: The image may be edited or selected and cannot represent the diversity of real bodies.
topics.explanation: A single idealised image does not provide a fair or accurate standard for everyone.
hints: Was the image necessarily an unedited everyday image?
Can one image represent all bodies?
topics.activity: Analyse a fictional text-only media claim for an implied appearance standard and write a respectful response; do not compare classmates' bodies.

topics.name: Seeking help in a water emergency
topics.description: In a water emergency, raising the alarm and seeking trained help are important. The safest response depends on the setting and a person's training; entering dangerous water can put another person at risk.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate seeking help in a water emergency using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Alert an adult, lifeguard or emergency service and stay in a safe place while seeking trained help.
misconceptions: The first response must always be to jump into the water.
topics.question: A fictional bystander sees someone in difficulty in water. What should they consider first?
topics.answer: Alert an adult, lifeguard or emergency service and stay in a safe place while seeking trained help.
topics.explanation: A safe alert can bring appropriate assistance without creating another person in danger.
hints: Who nearby is trained or able to call for help?
Where can the bystander stay safe?
topics.activity: Use an illustrated scenario to identify a safe location and an adult or emergency contact; do not stage a real rescue or enter water.

topics.name: Different purposes of sexual-health protection
topics.description: Contraceptive methods and abstinence can prevent unintended pregnancy, while barrier methods such as condoms also reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections. Methods differ, and a qualified health professional can discuss individual circumstances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 > Health, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate different purposes of sexual-health protection using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: No. Methods differ; barrier methods such as condoms can reduce STI risk, while some other contraceptive methods do not.
misconceptions: All contraception provides the same protection against infections.
topics.question: Does every contraceptive method reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections?
topics.answer: No. Methods differ; barrier methods such as condoms can reduce STI risk, while some other contraceptive methods do not.
topics.explanation: Pregnancy prevention and reducing infection risk are related but distinct purposes of sexual-health protection.
hints: Are all methods designed to do the same things?
Which type of method also provides a barrier against infection?
topics.activity: Compare fictional information cards for pregnancy and STI prevention using a reputable health source; do not ask learners about their own choices or experiences.

topics.name: Sexual-health information and services
topics.description: Sexually transmitted infections can affect health, and some do not produce obvious symptoms. Confidential health services can provide accurate information, testing and treatment appropriate to a person's circumstances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 > Health, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate sexual-health information and services using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Ask a qualified health service about appropriate information or testing.
misconceptions: A person who feels well can always tell that they do not have an STI.
topics.question: A fictional person wants to know whether an infection can be ruled out just because they feel well. What is a reliable next step?
topics.answer: Ask a qualified health service about appropriate information or testing.
topics.explanation: Symptoms alone do not reliably establish whether an infection is present; a health professional can advise on the situation.
hints: Do all infections always cause noticeable symptoms?
Who can provide confidential, individual advice?
topics.activity: Create a fictional resource list identifying how to access a trusted health service and the kinds of questions it can answer; no personal disclosure is needed.

topics.name: Recognising coercive control
topics.description: Coercion can involve threats, intimidation or pressure that restricts a person's ability to make decisions freely. Support from a trusted person or specialist service can help someone consider options safely.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26–27, Phase 4 > Health; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising coercive control using a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The threat uses pressure and isolation to restrict the person's choices and safety.
misconceptions: A threat is acceptable if someone says it proves they care.
topics.question: A fictional partner threatens to isolate someone from friends unless they obey. Why is this concerning?
topics.answer: The threat uses pressure and isolation to restrict the person's choices and safety.
topics.explanation: A healthy relationship respects boundaries and does not control access to support through threats.
hints: What happens if the person disagrees?
Does the threat leave them free to make their own choice?
topics.activity: Read a non-explicit fictional scenario and identify an example of pressure and a trusted support route; do not ask learners to disclose experiences.

topics.name: Leading an inclusive activity

topics.explanation: Changing the activity environment can remove a barrier without assuming that everyone moves in the same way.

How might naming it help the adult understand?

topics.name: Protecting skin, eyes and ears
topics.description: People can protect their bodies by making choices suited to a situation, such as seeking shade, using appropriate sun protection or moving away from a sound that is uncomfortably loud.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Physical and mental health: Body care, Phase 1 > Health, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate protecting skin, eyes and ears in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: They could seek shade and use appropriate sun protection with adult support.
misconceptions: Protection for skin, eyes and ears is only useful after someone is hurt.

What could provide shade or cover?

topics.name: Noticing effort and taking a break

evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Pause or adjust the activity and ask a trusted adult for support if needed.

topics.answer: Pause or adjust the activity and ask a trusted adult for support if needed.
topics.explanation: Noticing a body signal helps the player respond to their own needs rather than treating every body the same.
hints: What is the player noticing?
Could they take a break or make the activity gentler?

topics.name: Planning safe pool entry and exit

topics.answer: Listen to the instructor and identify the agreed safe entry and exit points.

Where does the group expect to enter and get out?

topics.name: Caring for outdoor places
topics.description: People can help protect outdoor places by taking rubbish away, staying on agreed paths and leaving plants and animals undisturbed. Local rules and tikanga can vary by place and should be checked with the people responsible for it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12, Active participation: Participating with others, Phase 1 > Physical Education, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate caring for outdoor places in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Ask an adult and place the wrapper in an appropriate rubbish bin or carry it out safely.

topics.answer: Ask an adult and place the wrapper in an appropriate rubbish bin or carry it out safely.
topics.explanation: Removing litter helps care for the place while avoiding unsafe or unknown objects.
hints: Does the wrapper belong on the ground?
Who can help decide how to dispose of it safely?
topics.activity: Sort drawn pictures of safe and unsafe litter actions and plan how a fictional group will leave a park tidy; do not collect unknown objects.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Changing hygiene needs in puberty
topics.description: As a body develops, hygiene needs can change, including how a person manages body odour. Needs and available resources differ, and questions about individual concerns can be taken to a trusted adult or health professional.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14–15, Physical and mental health: Body care and Puberty, Phase 2 > Health, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate changing hygiene needs in puberty in a relevant scenario.

topics.answer: They can consider a suitable hygiene routine and ask a trusted adult for help if needed.
topics.explanation: Changes in perspiration and body odour can occur during development, and support should respect privacy.

Who could help the student find suitable supplies or information?

topics.name: Sperm production and puberty

objectives: Explain or demonstrate sperm production and puberty in a relevant scenario.

misconceptions: Every person begins the same pubertal changes at exactly the same age.

topics.answer: The testes.

Which organs are named in the description?

topics.name: Menstruation and the uterine lining

objectives: Explain or demonstrate menstruation and the uterine lining in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The lining of the uterus is shed and leaves the body through the vagina.
misconceptions: Every person's menstrual cycle has exactly the same timing and symptoms.

topics.answer: The lining of the uterus is shed and leaves the body through the vagina.
topics.explanation: Menstruation is one part of a cycle that can vary between people and over time.
hints: Think about the organ called the uterus.
What happens to its lining during a period?
topics.activity: Use an age-appropriate, teacher-provided diagram to label uterus, lining and vagina, then write one respectful question for an information source without sharing personal details.

topics.name: Listening with empathy

topics.name: Breathing and swimming movement

topics.answer: Coordinating the movements helps the swimmer find a suitable moment to breathe and maintain a controlled stroke.
topics.explanation: Breathing and movement need to work together, and individual instruction adapts the technique to the learner and conditions.
hints: When must the mouth be clear of the water?
How could arm and body movement affect that moment?

topics.name: Pushes, pulls and movement

topics.answer: The rough mat can provide more friction that resists the ball's motion.

Which surface resists motion more in this example?

topics.name: Adapting a skill to a new game

topics.answer: They can use their aiming experience while changing their force and timing for the partner.

How is a moving or waiting partner different from a fixed target?

topics.name: Person, task and environment in movement

topics.name: Cardinal directions and simple wayfinding

topics.name: Power differences and consent
topics.description: A power difference can make it harder for someone to express a choice freely, especially when they fear a negative consequence. Clear information, respect for refusal and access to a safe support person can help.
