topics.name: Outdoor hazards and controls
topics.description: Outdoor safety planning considers hazards alongside controls such as route choice, supervision, equipment, communication and a decision to change or stop. The appropriate control depends on the group and the conditions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Active participation: Outdoor education, Phase 4 > Physical Education, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate outdoor hazards and controls in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Choose a more sheltered route or postpone, and agree on a decision point with the supervisor.
misconceptions: A safety plan only needs to name hazards and does not need actions to address them.
topics.question: A forecast shows rising wind before a fictional exposed ridge walk. What could the group plan?
topics.answer: Choose a more sheltered route or postpone, and agree on a decision point with the supervisor.
topics.explanation: Changing the route or timing can reduce exposure to a known hazard while the group monitors conditions.
hints: What hazard does the forecast suggest?
Which part of the plan could reduce exposure to that hazard?
topics.activity: On a fictional route map, list one hazard, one control and the point at which the group would reconsider the plan; do not attempt the route.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Reciprocity and outdoor stewardship
topics.description: People benefit from outdoor places and can also contribute to their care. Responsible actions depend on the place and may include following mana whenua guidance, minimising disturbance or joining a locally approved restoration activity.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Active participation: Outdoor education, Phase 4 > Physical Education, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate reciprocity and outdoor stewardship in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Follow local guidance and take an appropriate action to reduce its impact or support the reserve.
misconceptions: Enjoying an outdoor place creates no responsibility to care for it.
topics.question: A group enjoys visiting a reserve. What is one way it could give back to the place?
topics.answer: Follow local guidance and take an appropriate action to reduce its impact or support the reserve.
topics.explanation: Reciprocity involves both receiving benefits and accepting responsibility for care, with practices grounded in local context.
hints: How does the group benefit from the place?
Who can explain what care is appropriate there?
topics.activity: Create a fictional plan with one benefit received from a place and one locally guided action that supports its care; avoid disturbing plants or animals.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Seeking help about an unsafe secret
topics.description: A safe person respects a child's boundaries and listens when the child asks for help. If someone asks a child to keep a secret that feels unsafe or upsetting, the child can tell a trusted adult and keep seeking help if needed.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Relationships: Boundaries and safety, Phase 1 > Health, Year 1
objectives: Explain or demonstrate seeking help about an unsafe secret in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Tell a trusted adult or another safe support person, and keep seeking help if necessary.
misconceptions: A child must keep a secret even when they feel unsafe.
topics.question: A fictional child is told to keep an upsetting secret about someone's behaviour. What could the child do?
topics.answer: Tell a trusted adult or another safe support person, and keep seeking help if necessary.
topics.explanation: The child does not need to manage an unsafe situation alone, and a safe adult should listen and help.
hints: Is the child required to keep an unsafe secret?
Who could listen and help the child?
topics.activity: Use fictional role cards to identify two trusted support options and a simple sentence for asking for help; no personal stories are required.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Online recommendations and repeated content
topics.description: Online platforms can recommend more content based on what a user watches or interacts with. Recommendations can increase exposure to disturbing material; learners can stop viewing and seek help from a trusted adult.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Physical and mental health: Online safety, Phase 2 > Health, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate online recommendations and repeated content in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Stop viewing and ask a trusted adult for help with the recommendations or settings.
misconceptions: A recommended video must be safe and must be watched.
topics.question: A fictional app keeps suggesting upsetting videos after one is watched. What can the user do?
topics.answer: Stop viewing and ask a trusted adult for help with the recommendations or settings.
topics.explanation: A recommendation is a platform choice, not an instruction to keep watching; support can help reduce unwanted exposure.
hints: Does the user have to open every suggested video?
Who can help with upsetting content and settings?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional set of harmless video suggestions and use arrows to show how one topic might lead to more similar suggestions; identify a stop-and-seek-help choice.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Hormones and pubertal development
topics.description: Hormones are chemical messengers that help regulate many changes during puberty, including physical development and changes in sleep or emotional awareness. The timing and experience of these changes vary.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Physical and mental health: Puberty, Phase 3 > Health, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate hormones and pubertal development in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: They act as chemical messengers that help regulate changes in the body.
misconceptions: Puberty happens in exactly the same way and at the same time for everyone.
topics.question: What role do hormones have in pubertal development?
topics.answer: They act as chemical messengers that help regulate changes in the body.
topics.explanation: Puberty involves signals that influence development; a single experience or timeline does not apply to everyone.
hints: Are hormones messages sent within the body or rules made by classmates?
What do those signals help regulate?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional flow chart from a body signal to a possible general change and write that timing varies; learners do not need to share their own development.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Community responses to appearance pressure
topics.description: Appearance pressures can be addressed through individual, interpersonal and community actions. For example, peers can challenge harmful comments and a school can choose inclusive images and communication practices.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Physical and mental health: Mental health, Phase 4 > Health, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate community responses to appearance pressure in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Stop the ranking, use respectful and inclusive communication, and invite feedback about the account.
misconceptions: A person experiencing appearance pressure is solely responsible for changing the situation.
topics.question: A fictional school account posts edited images alongside comments ranking students' bodies. What could the school change?
topics.answer: Stop the ranking, use respectful and inclusive communication, and invite feedback about the account.
topics.explanation: Changing harmful practices addresses a source of pressure and supports a more inclusive environment.
hints: What is the account doing that could create pressure?
What can the people responsible for the account change?
topics.activity: Review a fictional text-only social media policy and propose one response to harmful comments and one way to make representation more inclusive; do not discuss classmates' bodies.

topics.name: Different kinds of family and whānau
topics.description: Families and whānau can have different members and ways of caring for one another. Respecting these differences helps people feel included; no learner needs to explain their own family circumstances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Relationships: Families and friendships, Phase 1 > Health, Year 1
objectives: Explain or demonstrate different kinds of family and whānau in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Both families deserve respect, and the children may be cared for in different ways.
misconceptions: Every family must have exactly the same members and routines.
topics.question: A fictional story shows two children living in different family arrangements. What respectful idea applies to both?
topics.answer: Both families deserve respect, and the children may be cared for in different ways.
topics.explanation: Family structures can differ without making one family's relationships less worthy of respect.
hints: Are all families made up in exactly the same way?
How can people respond respectfully to differences?
topics.activity: Read two fictional family descriptions and identify one respectful way to talk about each without asking learners to describe their own families.

topics.name: Joints and everyday movement
topics.description: A joint is a place where parts of the body meet and can allow movement such as bending. Different joints move in different ways, and activities can be adapted to an individual's comfort and ability.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Movement: The moving body, Phase 1 > Physical Education, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate joints and everyday movement in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The knee joint.
misconceptions: Every joint in the body moves in exactly the same way.
topics.question: Which body part can bend when a person moves a lower leg towards the upper leg?
topics.answer: The knee joint.
topics.explanation: The knee connects the upper and lower leg and allows a bending movement.
hints: Where do the upper and lower leg meet?
Which joint changes angle during the bend?
topics.activity: Use a simple diagram to mark the knee and elbow as joints, or gently show a comfortable movement without forcing a joint.
materials: simple body diagram or paper and pencil

topics.name: Landing with control
topics.description: Safe landing practice considers the surface, available space and each person's ability. In a suitable supervised activity, learners can explore a controlled, soft landing rather than rushing or forcing a movement.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Movement: Skill acquisition, Phase 1 > Physical Education, Year 1
objectives: Explain or demonstrate landing with control in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The group needs enough clear space and a suitable surface for the planned movement.
misconceptions: A landing is safe regardless of the surface or nearby people.
topics.question: Why should a group check its space and surface before practising landings?
topics.answer: The group needs enough clear space and a suitable surface for the planned movement.
topics.explanation: The environment and the participants' abilities affect whether a movement task is appropriate.
hints: Could objects or other people be in the way?
Who can help decide whether the surface and activity are suitable?
topics.activity: On paper, choose a clear, supervised landing area in a fictional gym picture; any physical practice should be gentle, adapted and led by an appropriate adult.

topics.name: Considering drink choices
topics.description: People's drink choices can be influenced by taste, availability, cost and advertising. Water is one possible everyday choice, while a label can give information about a packaged drink; circumstances and preferences differ.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Physical and mental health: Body care, Phase 2 > Health, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate considering drink choices in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Check the label and consider the advert's purpose alongside other available drink options.
misconceptions: An attractive advert proves a drink is the best choice for everyone.
topics.question: A colourful advert calls a sweet drink “the best”. What could a learner check before accepting the claim?
topics.answer: Check the label and consider the advert's purpose alongside other available drink options.
topics.explanation: A promotional claim is designed to persuade; the label and context provide more useful information about the choice.
hints: Who made the advert?
What factual information might be on the label?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional drink labels and circle one factual detail and one persuasive phrase; do not assess classmates' drinks or diets.

topics.name: Access and food choices
topics.description: Food choices depend partly on what is available and affordable, as well as preferences and whānau or cultural practices. Communities can look at practical barriers without blaming individuals or treating one family's food as the standard.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Physical and mental health: Body care, Phase 2 > Health, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate access and food choices in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Local availability and the difficulty of reaching a range of food options.
misconceptions: Food choices depend only on willpower and never on availability or cost.
topics.question: A fictional community has few nearby shops. What factor could affect food choices?
topics.answer: Local availability and the difficulty of reaching a range of food options.
topics.explanation: A person's choice depends partly on the options they can access, alongside other circumstances.
hints: What food options are nearby?
Does everyone have the same access to those options?
topics.activity: On a fictional map, mark a food shop and a distant neighbourhood, then suggest one community action that could improve access without making assumptions about residents.

topics.name: Food and body systems
topics.description: Food provides nutrients used by different body systems, including those involved in physical function and mental wellbeing. Needs and access vary, and one meal does not determine a person's health or feelings.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Physical and mental health: Body care, Phase 2 > Health, Year 6
objectives: Explain or demonstrate food and body systems in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Nutrients support different body systems and their functions.
misconceptions: A single food or meal guarantees how someone will feel or how healthy they are.
topics.question: Why does a growing body need nutrients from food?
topics.answer: Nutrients support different body systems and their functions.
topics.explanation: The body uses nutrients in multiple processes; a person's needs and overall circumstances can differ.
hints: Does food support only one part of the body?
What might the body use nutrients for as it grows and functions?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional diagram linking food to a body and two broad functions it supports; avoid analysing personal meals or assigning blame for food access.

topics.name: Wet dreams and variation in puberty
topics.description: Some people experience wet dreams during puberty, when semen is released during sleep. They are a possible developmental experience, but not everyone has them and their timing varies.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Physical and mental health: Puberty, Phase 2 > Health, Year 6
objectives: Explain or demonstrate wet dreams and variation in puberty in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Yes. Experiences and timing differ between people.
misconceptions: Every person must experience the same puberty changes at the same age.
topics.question: Is it possible for one person to have wet dreams during puberty while another does not?
topics.answer: Yes. Experiences and timing differ between people.
topics.explanation: A wet dream is one possible change, not a required sign that happens to everyone on the same schedule.
hints: Do all people experience the same changes?
Can a developmental experience vary from person to person?
topics.activity: Use a fictional question card to practise a respectful factual answer and identify a trusted source for private questions; no learner should be asked to disclose experiences.
materials: fictional question card and trusted age-appropriate source

topics.name: Variation in visible pubertal changes
topics.description: During puberty some people experience changes such as body hair, growth in height or voice changes. Which changes occur and when they occur vary, so comparisons between classmates are not reliable measures of development.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Physical and mental health: Puberty, Phase 2 > Health, Year 6
objectives: Explain or demonstrate variation in visible pubertal changes in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: No. The timing of pubertal changes varies between people.
misconceptions: Everyone develops each visible puberty change in the same order and at the same age.
topics.question: Two fictional students begin growing body hair at different times. Is that necessarily unusual?
topics.answer: No. The timing of pubertal changes varies between people.
topics.explanation: A single classmate's timeline is not a universal standard for another person's development.
hints: Do bodies develop on one fixed schedule?
Can different changes occur at different times?
topics.activity: Arrange fictional, non-personal development cards in two different possible orders, then note that individual pathways and timing vary; do not compare learners' bodies.

topics.name: Allergen information on food labels
topics.description: Food labels can include ingredient and allergen information that helps people identify items relevant to their needs. Labels and advice should be checked for the specific situation; a health professional can provide individual guidance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Physical and mental health: Nutrition, Phase 3 > Health, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate allergen information on food labels in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The ingredient list and any relevant allergen information.
misconceptions: A colourful package or advertisement gives all the information needed about ingredients.
topics.question: A fictional person needs to avoid a particular ingredient. What label information could help them check a packaged food?
topics.answer: The ingredient list and any relevant allergen information.
topics.explanation: These sections identify ingredients or declared allergens, helping the person find information relevant to their own needs.
hints: Where on a package are ingredients listed?
What other label information may identify allergens?
topics.activity: Compare two invented labels for a fictional ingredient and mark where the information appears; do not ask learners to disclose allergies or make a real medical decision.

topics.name: Recreation and organised sport
topics.description: People can take part in informal recreation or organised sport for many reasons, including enjoyment, social connection, skill development and competition. Access, culture and personal preferences can affect what is available and appealing.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Active participation: Social and cultural influences, Phase 3 > Physical Education, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recreation and organised sport in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The competition may have a formal schedule and rules, while the walk may be organised more informally.
misconceptions: Only competitive sport counts as meaningful physical activity.
topics.question: A nature walk and a table-tennis competition both involve movement. What is one possible difference?
topics.answer: The competition may have a formal schedule and rules, while the walk may be organised more informally.
topics.explanation: Activities can differ in organisation and purpose, although either can involve enjoyment, connection or skill.
hints: Which activity names a competition?
Could both still be enjoyable and social?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional activity descriptions by their organisation, possible purposes and access needs; do not rank participants' choices.

topics.name: Stressors and sources of support
topics.description: Stress can be influenced by personal circumstances, relationships and wider community events. Responses may include seeking support and considering changes to the stressor where possible; people differ in what helps.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Physical and mental health: Mental health, Phase 4 > Health, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate stressors and sources of support in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Discuss changing the deadline or workload and identify a trusted source of support.
misconceptions: Stress is always caused only by an individual's attitude.
topics.question: A fictional student feels pressure from an unrealistic group deadline. What could the group consider?
topics.answer: Discuss changing the deadline or workload and identify a trusted source of support.
topics.explanation: Addressing an external pressure as well as supporting the student can make the response more practical.
hints: What part of the situation creates pressure?
Can the group change the task rather than expecting one person to manage everything alone?
topics.activity: Analyse a fictional group deadline, label one source of pressure and propose one collective change and one support option; no personal disclosure is required.

topics.name: Protective factors and risk factors
topics.description: A protective factor can help a person manage a challenge, while a risk factor can make coping more difficult. Factors may be individual, relational or community-based, and they do not guarantee an outcome.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Physical and mental health: Mental health, Phase 4 > Health, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate protective factors and risk factors in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: The trusted mentor is a protective factor; the transport barrier can make participation harder.
misconceptions: A risk factor means an adverse outcome is certain.
topics.question: A fictional student has a trusted mentor and no safe transport to activities. Which is a protective factor?
topics.answer: The trusted mentor is a protective factor; the transport barrier can make participation harder.
topics.explanation: Supportive relationships can assist coping, while access barriers may increase difficulty; neither determines the person's future.
hints: Which part offers support?
Which part creates a barrier?
topics.activity: Create a fictional scenario and label one possible source of support and one barrier, then suggest a practical response without predicting an individual's health.

topics.name: Strength, endurance and flexibility
topics.description: Muscular strength describes the force muscles can produce, muscular endurance concerns sustaining repeated or prolonged effort, and flexibility concerns range of movement. Their relevance and expression vary across activities and people.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Movement: The moving body, Phase 4 > Physical Education, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate strength, endurance and flexibility in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Muscular endurance.
misconceptions: One fitness quality describes every kind of movement.
topics.question: Which term relates to sustaining repeated muscular effort: strength, endurance or flexibility?
topics.answer: Muscular endurance.
topics.explanation: Endurance concerns sustaining effort over time; strength and flexibility describe different qualities.
hints: Does the scenario emphasise one force, repeated effort or range of movement?
Which term describes keeping an effort going?
topics.activity: Match three fictional movement descriptions to strength, endurance and flexibility; use examples that allow seated or non-performing participation.

topics.name: Awareness of body position in movement
topics.description: Kinaesthetic awareness is a person's sense of their body's position, movement and effort. It can provide internal feedback that helps a learner adjust an action in a way suited to their own ability.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Movement: Skill acquisition, Phase 4 > Physical Education, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate awareness of body position in movement in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Their own awareness of body position and movement.
misconceptions: A learner can only know how they moved by watching a video.
topics.question: A learner notices that their arm moved too far during a gentle pass. What kind of information are they using?
topics.answer: Their own awareness of body position and movement.
topics.explanation: The observation comes from the learner's sense of their action rather than only from an external observer.
hints: Who noticed how the arm moved?
Does the information come from inside the learner's experience?
topics.activity: Use a fictional passing scenario to label one internal observation and one possible adjustment; no physical performance is required.

topics.name: Knowing where to get outdoor help
topics.description: Outdoor planning includes knowing who is responsible for help, how the group will communicate and what to do if someone needs assistance. A person should seek suitably qualified support and avoid taking actions beyond their training.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Active participation: Outdoor education, Phase 4 > Physical Education, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate knowing where to get outdoor help in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Alert the group leader and follow the agreed communication and support plan.
misconceptions: Anyone who notices an injury must perform a medical procedure regardless of training.
topics.question: A fictional walker is hurt and the group has a supervised plan. What should another participant do?
topics.answer: Alert the group leader and follow the agreed communication and support plan.
topics.explanation: A clear plan can bring qualified assistance while the group considers the safety of everyone involved.
hints: Who is responsible for leading the group response?
What communication method was agreed before the walk?
topics.activity: On a fictional route card, mark the leader, communication method and an appropriate help contact; do not practise medical procedures without a qualified instructor.

topics.name: Flotation equipment and supervision
topics.description: Water activities can require suitable, correctly fitted flotation equipment and qualified supervision. Equipment helps manage risk but does not make every water environment safe or replace instruction.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17–18, Movement: Water safety, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate flotation equipment and supervision in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: To make sure the equipment is suitable and fitted for the activity and participant.
misconceptions: Wearing flotation equipment removes the need for supervision or attention to conditions.
topics.question: Why should a group check flotation equipment before a supervised activity?
topics.answer: To make sure the equipment is suitable and fitted for the activity and participant.
topics.explanation: Appropriate equipment is one part of a safety plan that also considers conditions, supervision and individual needs.
hints: Does one size necessarily fit every participant?
What else besides equipment is needed for a safe plan?
topics.activity: Use an illustrated equipment checklist for a fictional supervised activity, including fit, conditions and the instructor; do not enter water for this task.

topics.name: Cold water and safe planning
topics.description: Water temperature can influence safety and movement. A supervised group should consider local conditions, suitable equipment and whether an activity should proceed; cold-water survival positions are taught by qualified instructors in appropriate settings.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Movement: Water safety, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate cold water and safe planning in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Ask the qualified supervisor to reassess conditions, equipment and whether the activity is appropriate.
misconceptions: Water temperature cannot affect safety if the weather is sunny.
topics.question: A fictional group learns that the water is colder than expected. What should it do before proceeding?
topics.answer: Ask the qualified supervisor to reassess conditions, equipment and whether the activity is appropriate.
topics.explanation: Temperature is one factor in the group's risk assessment, and a supervisor can adapt or stop the plan.
hints: What has changed in the environment?
Who can decide whether the planned activity remains suitable?
topics.activity: Review a fictional water-activity plan and mark temperature, supervision and a decision point; do not practise in cold water for this task.

topics.name: Different swimming strokes and conditions
topics.description: Swimming strokes use different coordinated body, arm, leg and breathing actions. A qualified instructor can help a learner select and practise an appropriate stroke in a suitable supervised setting.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Movement: Water safety, Phase 2 > Physical Education; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate different swimming strokes and conditions in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: Different strokes use different movements and can be suited to different learning goals or conditions.
misconceptions: Knowing the name of a stroke proves that someone can perform it safely in open water.
topics.question: Why might a swimmer learn more than one stroke?
topics.answer: Different strokes use different movements and can be suited to different learning goals or conditions.
topics.explanation: A wider range of taught movements gives a learner options, while their safe use depends on instruction and the setting.
hints: Do all strokes use identical movements?
Who can help a learner practise a stroke safely?
topics.activity: Compare two instructor-provided diagrams of swimming strokes and label one visible difference; any water practice requires qualified supervision.

topics.name: Attacking and defending in modified games
topics.description: Game tactics can include moving to keep possession or create an opportunity, and responding to prevent the other group from doing so. Rules, communication and safe space should suit the participants and the game.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Active participation: Participating with others, Phase 2 > Physical Education, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate attacking and defending in modified games in a relevant scenario.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the scenario: It is a defending action in this example.
misconceptions: A team uses tactics only when it has the object.
topics.question: In a fictional passing game, a player moves to intercept an opponent's pass. Is that attacking or defending?
topics.answer: It is a defending action in this example.
topics.explanation: The player is trying to prevent the other group from completing its pass.
hints: Which group currently has the object?
Is the player trying to keep possession or interrupt the other group's pass?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional passing game with players as counters, then mark one possible attacking pass and one safe defending position.
